rv.q: This British version is the most merciless and empathic interpretation of this much performed work I’ve seen, and it keeps returning to my thoughts in piercing shards, like the remnants of a too-revealing dream.

Aching, wistful and wounding, the director’s staging of Betrayal presents three friends and lovers trapped in an undoing of their own making, their inevitable self-destruction no less powerful for showing itself before the happier days.
The balance of complex psychological drama, pervasive melancholy and acid humor is riveting.
The three performers bring such emotional precision to Harold Pinter's reverse-chronology tale of adultery that you feel you're witnessing something profound about the nature of intimacy.
Of all Pinter’s often-puzzling work, this play is the one that clearly speaks to you, thinks for you, and may even feel for you.
And yet it also understands that infidelity has a sweet and gentle side.
At its best, the play is white-hot.
This production of Harold Pinter's 'Betrayal' is a sleek, sophisticated rendering of the playwright's examination of infidelity and friendship.
You can feel, as I did, like you’re watching Acting Well, which is a matter of intellect rather than emotion.

Even in sure-footed ventures into the Pinterverse—such as Jamie Lloyd’s lean and sexy revival starring Tom Hiddleston, now visiting New York after its London premiere—there can be an element of technical gloss to contend with.
It was a strange and incongruous moment, and it provided a welcome burst of surprise in a production that is otherwise a chic and dreary affair.
They're fine, maybe even better than that, but the play and production don't test them.
Bottom line: Best Broadway revival of a Harold Pinter drama in over a decade.
That’s the brilliance of Lloyd’s can’t-miss revival.
Lloyd's production is likewise interested in such negative space, resulting in a Betrayal that rewards looking closely.
What could so easily come off like soap opera in lesser hands rises in this production to the level of modern tragedy.

There is certainly a beautiful, open elegance to Lloyd’s production that echoes its three supremely fine performances and a reading of the text that pinpoints all of Pinter’s wit, wordplay, and mordancy, while leaving a lovely breadth of interpretation open to the audience.
Director Jamie Lloyd's Subtle Way With Harold Pinter's 'BETRAYAL'
Jamie Lloyd's staging lays bare the play's elegant bones, the tightly knotted network of lies and evasions.
Betrayal is an unembellished marvel and this Broadway revival gives the 1978 play a smart, stripped down treatment.
The present production, thanks to Lloyd and his acting company, demonstrates that after 40 years, Pinter’s examination of truth and deception holds up exceedingly well.
To borrow an art-world term, her work is “counterfeit.”
Lloyd strips the play to its essentials and gets at the heart of Pinter’s portrait of easy deception and the pain it causes.
It's that kind of fogginess that finally makes this production only intermittently memorable and rarely revelatory.
The revelation for me is how little I could embrace a production so many others have admired, of a play whose subtleties I’ve appreciated in the past, and not just on paper.
Upon further study, I'm sure mountains of subtext can be excavated from each interaction, but in the moment, they offer little reason to emotionally buy in.

To Lloyd's credit, and that of this spectacular cast, we never lose sight of the ways in which these three lives are ineradicably interwoven, giving more power to the emptiness and emotional wreckage their actions have wrought – despite their best attempts to be so very British about it all.
In fact, the brilliance of the acting here in Jamie Lloyd’s unconventionally minimalist, finely tuned staging only serves to emphasize the play’s technical glitter over its emotional heartbeat.
She hardly seems worth anyone’s trouble, and I’m not sure the play does either.

tn.cat: Best Scenic Design of a Play

cn.t: Jamie Lloyd's stripped-down revival of Pinter's infidelity drama earns strong praise for its surgical precision and stellar performances from Hiddleston, Cox, and Ashton, though some critics find the cool, minimalist approach emotionally remote.

sg.ra: Wikipedia confirms the Jacobs orchestra floor is raked and the house has a single balcony (not two), so Center Orchestra rows A-D get close detail without the second-balcony crush. Playbill's Outsiders guide names Orchestra C Row B Seat 112 the best seat in the house; SeatPlan and Headout both call rows A-D the premium pick for plays specifically. Row numbering 101-114 (center block) means 107/108 sit dead-center on the aisle.

Multiple guides single out Center Orchestra rows F-K as the Jacobs value play: same centered sightline as the A-D premium block, but priced well below because Row I is where the mezzanine overhang line starts (overhead, not yet cutting into the stage). The Jacobs' single-balcony design and raked orchestra floor keep these rows clear, and Wikipedia notes two columns at the rear-of-orchestra promenade supporting the balcony - those sit behind Row N/O, so F-N stay clear of the columns.

SeatPlan and Headout both say the mezzanine overhang 'cuts into the top of the stage' starting at Row O - this is the Jacobs' specific geometry (mezz front at Row I, stage-top cutoff at Row O). Wikipedia adds that the rear-orchestra promenade has two columns supporting the balcony, so patrons here also share space with structural posts. Wheelchair spaces are assigned to rows I, J, P, and R per Headout, confirming P/R are flat promenade rows.

sg.vl: Fine if you pick single-digit seats
sg.ra: Side orchestra uses odd 1-27 (Left) and even 2-28 (Right). SeatPlan notes sightline restrictions intensify at double-digit seats (far aisle) and in back rows. Playbill's Outsiders guide specifically flagged that the right-side front rows were 'a clearer view' than left, because the show's tire set piece on house-left obstructs Orchestra L front rows - this is show-dependent but illustrates the Jacobs' shallow thrust style where side props block near side-orch seats. An AVFMS Orchestra G17 reviewer wrote 'sometimes the boxes block your view of the jungle gym' - the side boxes eat into side-orch sightlines.

sg.vl: Sharp angle, sells as obstructed for a reason
sg.ra: The Jacobs has 2 box seats on each side (16 total per Wikipedia) elevated beside the orchestra. TripAdvisor's theatre rep confirmed obstructed-view seats cluster 'on the extreme sides of the front mezzanine and orchestra' - the boxes are the prime example. Multiple guides warn boxes 'cut off high center stage scenes' and block views of stage-left from the right box / stage-right from the left box. SeatPlan explicitly recommends left boxes over right because the right box loses more stage-left content.

sg.vl: Elevated wide view, 9 rows from stage
sg.ra: SeatPlan names Center Mezz rows A-B the best mezz view in the Jacobs; an AVFMS reviewer at Mezz A107 wrote 'you are perfectly centered and at only nine rows from the stage' - the Jacobs' single-balcony design (per Wikipedia, no second balcony) means the mezz sits close rather than stacked high. Row B dodges Row A's safety-bar issue that SeatPlan calls 'obstructive to shorter patrons.' Front mezz is 168 seats in rows A-D with premium centered sightlines on the full set.

sg.vl: Row E is the legroom hack
sg.ra: Rear mezz is 252 seats in rows E-K. The Jacobs-specific quirk: Row E sits directly behind the front-mezz cross-aisle with a curtain/bannister (not a wall), giving 'extra space' for taller patrons per SeatPlan - Playbill's Outsiders guide confirms Mezz Left Row E has 'a curtained divider between the aisle and row' for extra legroom. Rows G-K are flagged as value seats because the mezz has a 'good rake' and Wikipedia confirms the Jacobs has only one balcony so even Row K stays surprisingly close. An AVFMS Mezz H22 reviewer noted 'legroom is not great' - stick to Row E or aisle seats.
